newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOJ governor says hopes baht will stabilise soon.
newsitem.headline: BOJ governor says hopes baht will stabilise soon.

text.p: Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita told a news conference on Wednesday that he hopes the Thai baht will stabilise quickly.

"The Thai authorities raised the official discount rate two percentage points. At the same time, they moved to a managed floating system (for the baht). These will contribute to improving its current account balance, together with the weakening of the baht," Matsushita said.
"I hope that Thailand will be able to regain stability in its currency soon," he added.
Matsushita said he would like to refrain from commenting on financial support for Thailand from Japan.
When he meets with the Thai central bank governor later this week, he expects his counterpart to explain recent economic conditions and currency movements, he said.
"But this is not a type of meeting where we decide beforehand what is going to be discussed, so I will not make any further comments on this," he said.

The rise in Japan's current account surplus in April and May was due to weakness in the yen, strong economies abroad and manufacturers increasing exports back to levels seen last year, Matsushita said.
Several manufacturers reduced exports in the January-March quarter of this year, due to heightened domestic demand ahead of the April 1 increase in Japan's national sales tax.
"The surplus is likely to remain at levels seen in April and May, but there are also dampening factors, such as the recent strength of the yen and Japan's economic recovery," Matsushita said.
"It is difficult to predict if the surplus will continue to rise (in the longer term)," he said.
He added that growth in Japan's net exports was one factor that triggered a favourable chain of events in the private sector economy.
Matsushita said that recent strength in the yen may have a dampening impact on Japan's exports in the medium- to long-term, but it is hard to predict how other factors may affect exports.

Matsushita said he felt that what was currently happening to several Asian currencies stemmed from decisions by authorities in those countries that they need to gradually adjust, in a long time frame, their currency system.
